original-en.context: Suppliants of all ages are seated round the altar at the palace doors, at their head a PRIEST OF ZEUS. To them enter OEDIPUS.

modern-en.context: OEDIPUS. My children, the youngest descendants of ancient Cadmus, why do you sit here as suppliants, holding in your hands olive branches wreathed with wool? Why is the whole city filled with the smell of incense, and echoing everywhere with lamentations and prayers? Children, I did not think it right to learn of this from others, so I have come here myself, I, Oedipus, your world-renowned king. You there — old man — whose venerable white hair marks you as the spokesman of this gathering, tell me your mood and your purpose. Is it dread of some evil that moves you, or do you come asking a favor? You cannot doubt my zeal on your behalf; I would be ruthless and hard-hearted indeed if I turned away petitioners such as you.

original-en.context: CHORUS. Cease, princes; lo there comes, and none too soon, Jocasta from the palace. Who so fit As peacemaker to reconcile your feud?

modern-en.context: CHORUS. Stop, my princes — look, here, and none too soon, comes Jocasta from the palace. Who is better fitted than she to settle your quarrel?

original-en.context: OEDIPUS. Ah! my poor children, known, ah, known too well, The quest that brings you hither and your need. Ye sicken all, well wot I, yet my pain, How great soever yours, outtops it all. Your sorrow touches each man severally, Him and none other, but I grieve at once Both for the general and myself and you. Therefore ye rouse no sluggard from day-dreams. Many, my children, are the tears I’ve wept, And threaded many a maze of weary thought. Thus pondering one clue of hope I caught, And tracked it up; I have sent Menoeceus’ son, Creon, my consort’s brother, to inquire Of Pythian Phoebus at his Delphic shrine, How I might save the State by act or word. And now I reckon up the tale of days Since he set forth, and marvel how he fares. ’Tis strange, this endless tarrying, passing strange. But when he comes, then I were base indeed, If I perform not all the god declares.

modern-en.context: OEDIPUS. My poor children — I know well, all too well, the mission that brings you here and what you need. I am aware that you are all sick, and yet, however great your pain, mine is greater still. Your sorrow touches each of you alone, him and no other; but I grieve at once for the city, for myself, and for you. So you have not roused a sluggard from his daydreams. Many are the tears I have shed, my children, and many are the tangled paths of thought I have wandered. Weighing all this, I found one thread of hope and followed it up: I have sent Menoeceus' son, Creon, my wife's brother, to consult Pythian Phoebus at his Delphic shrine, to learn how I might save the state by deed or word. And now, counting up the days since he set out, I wonder at his delay. It is strange, this endless tarrying, strange indeed. But when he arrives, I would be vile indeed if I failed to do everything the god commands.

original-en.context: PRIEST. Yea, Oedipus, my sovereign lord and king, Thou seest how both extremes of age besiege Thy palace altars—fledglings hardly winged, and greybeards bowed with years; priests, as am I of Zeus, and these the flower of our youth. Meanwhile, the common folk, with wreathed boughs Crowd our two market-places, or before Both shrines of Pallas congregate, or where Ismenus gives his oracles by fire. For, as thou seest thyself, our ship of State, Sore buffeted, can no more lift her head, Foundered beneath a weltering surge of blood. A blight is on our harvest in the ear, A blight upon the grazing flocks and herds, A blight on wives in travail; and withal Armed with his blazing torch the God of Plague Hath swooped upon our city emptying The house of Cadmus, and the murky realm Of Pluto is full fed with groans and tears. Therefore, O King, here at thy hearth we sit, I and these children; not as deeming thee A new divinity, but the first of men; First in the common accidents of life, And first in visitations of the Gods. Art thou not he who coming to the town of Cadmus freed us from the tax we paid To the fell songstress? Nor hadst thou received Prompting from us or been by others schooled; No, by a god inspired (so all men deem, And testify) didst thou renew our life. And now, O Oedipus, our peerless king, All we thy votaries beseech thee, find Some succor, whether by a voice from heaven Whispered, or haply known by human wit. Tried counselors, methinks, are aptest found To furnish for the future pregnant rede. Upraise, O chief of men, upraise our State! Look to thy laurels! for thy zeal of yore Our country’s savior thou art justly hailed: O never may we thus record thy reign:— “He raised us up only to cast us down.” Uplift us, build our city on a rock. Thy happy star ascendant brought us luck, O let it not decline! If thou wouldst rule This land, as now thou reignest, better sure To rule a peopled than a desert realm. Nor battlements nor galleys aught avail, If men to man and guards to guard them tail.

modern-en.context: PRIEST. Yes, Oedipus, my sovereign lord and king, you can see for yourself how both extremes of age crowd the altars at your palace — young children barely fledged, and old men bent with years; priests, as I am of Zeus, and these, the flower of our youth. Meanwhile the common people, carrying wreathed branches, throng our two market squares, or gather before the twin shrines of Pallas, or where Ismenus gives his oracles by fire. For, as you yourself see, our ship of state, battered by storms, can no longer lift her head — she is foundering beneath a surging tide of blood. A blight has struck the ears of our corn, a blight has struck our grazing flocks and herds, a blight has struck our women in childbirth; and over all this, armed with his blazing torch, the God of Plague has swooped down on our city, emptying the house of Cadmus, while the dark kingdom of Pluto is glutted with groans and tears. That is why, O King, we sit here at your hearth, I and these children — not because we think you a new god, but because we believe you first among men; first in the ordinary misfortunes of life, and first in what the gods send down on us. Are you not the one who came to the town of Cadmus and freed us from the tribute we paid to that cruel songstress? You had no prompting from us, nor any lesson from others; no, it was by a god's inspiration (so all men believe, and bear witness) that you restored our lives. And now, O Oedipus, our peerless king, all of us, your worshippers, beg you to find some remedy — whether through a voice whispered from heaven, or through what a man's wit can discover. Tried counselors, I think, are best equipped to suggest what will come of the future. Lift up our state, O first of men, lift it up! Watch over your good name, for because of your past devotion our country hails you, justly, as its savior. Never let this be said of your reign: 'He raised us up only to cast us down.' Lift us up, build our city on a rock. Your lucky star ascending brought us good fortune once — oh, do not let it set now! If you wish to rule this land, as you now reign, it is surely better to rule a peopled kingdom than an empty one. Neither walls nor ships are worth anything if the men inside them fail.
